claim: An expanded GGGGCC hexanucleotide in C9ORF72 (C9) is the most frequent known cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
source: An expanded GGGGCC hexanucleotide in C9ORF72 (C9) is the most frequent known cause of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations in the introduction (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011).

claim: The protein that predominantly associates with GGGGCC repeat RNA in vitro is the splicing factor hnRNP H.
source: Here we show first that the protein that predominantly associates with GGGGCC repeat RNA in vitro is the splicing factor hnRNP H, and that this interaction is linked to G-Q formation.
evidence: Demonstrated through UV-crosslinking experiments showing hnRNP H as the major crosslinked protein (Figure 1, Figure 2).

claim: The interaction between hnRNP H and GGGGCC repeat RNA is linked to G-quadruplex (G-Q) formation.
source: Here we show first that the protein that predominantly associates with GGGGCC repeat RNA in vitro is the splicing factor hnRNP H, and that this interaction is linked to G-Q formation.
evidence: Supported by experiments using 7-deaza GTP to destabilize G-Q structures and BG4 antibody immunoprecipitation (Figure 1).

claim: G-Q RNA foci are more abundant in C9 ALS patient fibroblasts and astrocytes compared to those without the expansion.
source: We then show that G-Q RNA foci are more abundant in C9 ALS patient fibroblasts and astrocytes compared to those without the expansion, and more frequently colocalize with hnRNP H.
evidence: Quantified using BG4 antibody staining and the BG4 Count program (Figure 3).

claim: G-Q RNA foci more frequently colocalize with hnRNP H in C9 ALS patient cells compared to control cells.
source: We then show that G-Q RNA foci are more abundant in C9 ALS patient fibroblasts and astrocytes compared to those without the expansion, and more frequently colocalize with hnRNP H.
evidence: Demonstrated through immunofluorescence colocalization studies (Figure 4).

claim: Multiple known hnRNP H-target transcripts show dysregulated splicing in C9 patient brains.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate dysregulated splicing of multiple known hnRNP H-target transcripts in C9 patient brains, which correlates with elevated insoluble hnRNP H/G-Q aggregates.
evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis of alternative splicing events in cerebellum samples (Figure 5).

claim: Dysregulated splicing of hnRNP H-target transcripts correlates with elevated insoluble hnRNP H/G-Q aggregates in C9 patient brains.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate dysregulated splicing of multiple known hnRNP H-target transcripts in C9 patient brains, which correlates with elevated insoluble hnRNP H/G-Q aggregates.
evidence: Demonstrated through biochemical fractionation and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 6).

claim: C9 expansion-mediated sequestration of hnRNP H is a significant contributor to neurodegeneration in C9 ALS/FTD.
source: Together, our data implicate C9 expansion-mediated sequestration of hnRNP H as a significant contributor to neurodegeneration in C9 ALS/FTD.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Expansion of a hexanucleotide, GGGGCC (G4C2) occurs in an intervening sequence separating two putative first, noncoding exons in the gene C9ORF72.
source: Expansion of a hexanucleotide, GGGGCC (G4C2) in an intervening sequence separating two putative first, noncoding exons in the gene C9ORF72 (C9) (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011) is the most frequent known cause of both disorders.
evidence: Cited from foundational studies (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Renton et al., 2011).

claim: The existence of ribonucleoprotein inclusions involving the RNA binding proteins TDP-43 or FUS in the brains and spinal cords of nearly all ALS patients suggests that defects in RNA processing lead to neurodegeneration.
source: The existence of ribonucleoprotein inclusions involving the RNA binding proteins TDP-43 or FUS in the brains and spinal cords of nearly all ALS patients and the occurrence of ALS-causing mutations in their respective genes (Ling et al., 2013) suggest that defects in RNA processing lead to neurodegeneration.
evidence: Based on established observations in the field and cited literature (Ling et al., 2013).

claim: Sequestration of RNA-binding proteins by the transcribed G4C2 expansion is a proposed pathogenic mechanism in C9ALS.
source: In the case of C9ALS, sequestration of RNA-binding proteins by the transcribed G4C2 expansion is a proposed pathogenic mechanism, and it has been shown that RNA from this locus forms intranuclear foci in the brains of affected individuals (Donnelly et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous work (Donnelly et al., 2013).

claim: RNA from the C9ORF72 locus forms intranuclear foci in the brains of affected individuals.
source: In the case of C9ALS, sequestration of RNA-binding proteins by the transcribed G4C2 expansion is a proposed pathogenic mechanism, and it has been shown that RNA from this locus forms intranuclear foci in the brains of affected individuals (Donnelly et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous work (Donnelly et al., 2013).

claim: Poly dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins are translated from repeat-containing transcripts.
source: It has also been shown that poly dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins are translated from repeat-containing transcripts, and DPRs may contribute toxic effects of their own (Mori et al., 2013b; Kwon et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Mori et al., 2013b; Kwon et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2014).

claim: DPRs may contribute toxic effects of their own.
source: It has also been shown that poly dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins are translated from repeat-containing transcripts, and DPRs may contribute toxic effects of their own (Mori et al., 2013b; Kwon et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Mori et al., 2013b; Kwon et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2014).

claim: Expansion length is variable, with expansions above an indeterminate threshold (~30–40, but up to several thousand) causing disease.
source: First, expansion length is variable, with expansions above an indeterminate threshold (~30–40, but up to several thousand) causing disease (Nordin et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous work (Nordin et al., 2015).

claim: The sequence of the C9 expansion favors formation of an especially stable G quadruplex (G-Q) structure.
source: Second, the sequence of the expansion favors formation of an especially stable G quadruplex (G-Q) structure, which consists of planar tetrad arrays of four non-sequential guanosine residues connected by Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds.
evidence: Based on known properties of G-quadruplex structures and the GGGGCC sequence.

claim: A G-quadruplex structure consists of planar tetrad arrays of four non-sequential guanosine residues connected by Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds.
source: Second, the sequence of the expansion favors formation of an especially stable G quadruplex (G-Q) structure, which consists of planar tetrad arrays of four non-sequential guanosine residues connected by Hoogsteen hydrogen bonds.
evidence: This is a standard definition of G-quadruplex structures.

claim: Two or more planar G-tetrad arrays interact through pi-pi stacking, stabilized by a central monovalent cation, generally potassium.
source: Two or more of these planar arrays then interact through pi-pi stacking, stabilized by a central monovalent cation, generally potassium (Davis, 2004).
evidence: Cited from previous work (Davis, 2004).

claim: Independent G-Qs can stack upon each other, forming higher order multimers.
source: Independent G-Qs can stack upon each other, forming higher order multimers.
evidence: This is a known property of G-quadruplex structures.

claim: Stability of G-Q structures is greater for RNA versus equivalent DNA structures.
source: For example, stability is greater for RNA versus equivalent DNA structures, reflecting the presence of 2' hydroxyls that participate in H-bonds within the RNA quadruplex (Collie et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from previous work (Collie et al., 2011).

claim: Four quartet G-Qs are substantially more stable than their three quartet counterparts.
source: Furthermore, four quartet G-Qs, such as the O. nova telomeric sequence (GGGGTTTT)n, are substantially more stable than their three quartet human telomeric counterparts, which in turn are more stable than G-Qs with two quartets (Lee et al., 2008; Mullen et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Lee et al., 2008; Mullen et al., 2012).

claim: It has been proposed that G-Q formation is a significant aspect of the toxicity of the repeats in ALS/FTD.
source: It has been proposed that G-Q formation is a significant aspect of the toxicity of the repeats in ALS/FTD (Haeusler et al., 2014; Simone et al., 2015), but whether such structures are indeed prevalent in C9 ALS/FTD patient brains, and if so, whether, and how, they are pathogenic in ALS/FTD has not been determined.
evidence: Cited from previous work (Haeusler et al., 2014; Simone et al., 2015).

claim: UV-crosslinking of 10R RNA to U87 nuclear extract produces two predominant bands at ~60–65 kDa and ~75 kDa.
source: We consistently observed two predominant bands, one of ~60–65 kDa and one ~75 kDa (Figure 1a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The crosslinked RNA-protein complexes from 10R are unaffected by RNAse A, T1 or both.
source: Unexpectedly, these species were unaffected by RNAse A, T1 or both (Figure 1a, lanes 2–5), with the only difference being that in the absence of RNAse, a band appeared at the top of the gel, possibly reflecting higher-order aggregates that failed to migrate into the gel (lane 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1a, lanes 2-5.

claim: Free 10R RNA resolves into two bands on SDS PAGE.
source: Notably, although the RNA alone ran as a single band of the predicted size on denaturing urea PAGE (Figure 1b, lanes 1 and 5, bottom), on SDS PAGE the free RNA gave rise to two bands, one at the expected MW of the full-length RNA (~20–25 kDa, based on protein markers), and a lower band that migrated faster (~15 kDa) (Figure 1a, lane 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1a, lane 1 and Figure 1b.

claim: Both 10R RNA species resolved by SDS PAGE contain G-Qs.
source: On denaturing PAGE, full-length RNA was detected following IP, consistent with the presence of G-Q (lane 5, bottom). On nondenaturing PAGE, both products were recovered following IP (lane 5, top), indicating that both species contain G-Qs.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1b using BG4 antibody immunoprecipitation.

claim: The two 10R species resolved by nondenaturing PAGE reflect two distinct G-Q states.
source: We conclude that the two 10R species resolved by nondenaturing PAGE reflect two distinct G-Q states, e.g., one in which four G4C2 tracts form one G-Q, and the other in which eight tracts form two G-Qs (Figure 1c).
evidence: Inferred from BG4 IP results (Figure 1b) and illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Heating 10R to 95°C slightly reduces the appearance of the crosslinked doublet.
source: Heating 10R slightly reduced the appearance of the crosslinked doublet, leading to a corresponding increase of a band at ~50 kDa (compare lanes 1 and 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1d, lanes 1 and 3.

claim: Crosslinking of 10R-7dG is substantially reduced relative to 10R even without heating.
source: More striking results were observed with 10R-7dG. Even in the absence of heating, crosslinking to produce the high MW doublet was substantially reduced relative to 10R (lane 2), supporting the view that these species represent protein binding to G-Q RNA.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1d, lane 2.

claim: Heating 10R-7dG abolishes appearance of the doublet and produces strong crosslinking at ~50 kDa.
source: Strikingly, heating 10R-7dG abolished appearance of the doublet and produced strong crosslinking that gave rise to the ~50 kDa species (lane 4).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1d, lane 4.

claim: The only free RNA that underwent significant RNAse degradation was heated 10R-7dG.
source: Notably, the only free RNA (at the bottom of the gel) that underwent significant RNAse degradation was heated 10R-7dG (lane 4), consistent with the idea that RNAse resistance reflects stable G-Q structures.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1d, lane 4.

claim: Heated 10R-G results in nearly complete loss of the doublet and appearance of increased amounts of the 50 kDa species.
source: However, heated 10R-G resulted in the nearly complete loss of the doublet and appearance of increased amounts of the 50 kDa species (and fainter band beneath), as well as a reduction in intensity of the upper free RNA species (lane 5).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1e, lane 5.

claim: Unheated 10R-G-7dG shows much higher levels of 50 kDa bands than 10R.
source: With unheated 10R-G-7dG we observed much higher levels of 50 kDa bands than with 10R (compare lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1e, lanes 2 and 4.

claim: Heating 10R-G in 0.1 M KCl leads to less crosslinking at 50 kDa and reappearance of the higher MW doublet.
source: We predict that in neurons, sequestration of hnRNP H becomes more severe with time and continuing C9 transcription, until functional levels become low enough to deregulate splicing, providing an explanation for the age dependence of ALS/FTD.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1e, lane 7.

claim: The crosslinked species at ~50 kDa represents hnRNP H.
source: Several lines of evidence, including the size of the 'denatured' crosslinked species (~50 kDa) and known affinity for poly(rG), led us to hypothesize that it may be the splicing regulator hnRNP H (Caputi and Zahler, 2002; Chou et al., 1999; Dardenne et al., 2014; Fisette et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on molecular weight and known binding properties, confirmed by IP experiments (Figure 2).

claim: Both the major and minor 50 kDa crosslinked species from 10R-7dG are immunoprecipitated by hnRNP H antibody.
source: With 10R-7dG, the major and minor 50 kDa crosslinked species described above were IPed, but the more abundant higher MW species again were not (lane 8).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2b, lane 8.

claim: The higher MW doublet from 10R crosslinking represents hnRNP H, but the structured RNA obstructs recognition by hnRNP H antibody.
source: Nonetheless, we believe this doublet does in fact represent hnRNP H, but the structured nature of the RNA that enables the complex to resist RNAse degradation (Figure 1a) also obstructs recognition by hnRNP H antibody (see also below).
evidence: Inferred from the combination of crosslinking and IP results.

claim: Crosslinking with purified H1 produces a single species running slightly above 50 kDa after RNAse treatment.
source: Crosslinking with purified H1 followed by RNAse treatment led to a single species running slightly above 50 kDa (lane 1), reflecting the ~4 kDa affinity tag on H1.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2d, lane 1.

claim: When products are not treated with RNAse, both H1 and NE produce highly similar patterns of doublets.
source: However, when products were not treated with RNAse, both H1 and NE produced highly similar patterns of doublets, as well as lower mobility species that failed to migrate into the gel, likely reflecting larger multimers as observed above (Figure 2b, lane 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2d, lanes 2 and 4.

claim: siRNA-mediated depletion of hnRNP H reduces formation of the crosslinked doublet.
source: Importantly, both species in the crosslinked doublet, as well as the band at the top of the gel, were significantly reduced in siH NE relative to the amount detected in siNC NE (Figure 2F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2F.

claim: hnRNP H is the predominant, and perhaps only, protein in U87 NE to crosslink to 10R.
source: We conclude that hnRNP H is the predominant, and perhaps only, protein in U87 NE to crosslink to 10R and that the variations in mobility reflect differential G-Q formation and/or stability.
evidence: Based on the combined crosslinking, IP, and knockdown experiments.

claim: The KD for the interaction between H1 and 4R is 75.5 ± 14 nM.
source: From these assays, we estimated the KD for the interaction between H1 and 4R to be 75.5 ± 14 nM, while the affinity of H1 for 4R-7dG was significantly higher, with a KD of 13.5±3.0 nM.
evidence: Determined from gel shift assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The affinity of H1 for 4R-7dG is significantly higher than for 4R, with a KD of 13.5±3.0 nM.
source: From these assays, we estimated the KD for the interaction between H1 and 4R to be 75.5 ± 14 nM, while the affinity of H1 for 4R-7dG was significantly higher, with a KD of 13.5±3.0 nM.
evidence: Determined from gel shift assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: C9ALS patient fibroblasts contain on average 1.8 times as many G-Q foci as control cells.
source: This indicated that, on average, patient cells contained 1.8 times as many G-Q foci as control cells, with a false discovery rate of less than 0.1% (Figure 3c).
evidence: Quantified using BG4 Count program on immunofluorescence images (Figure 3).

claim: C9ALS patient astrocytes have 2.0 times as many G-Q foci as control astrocytes.
source: Likewise, comparison of one C9ALS patient astrocyte line and one control over three separate experiments (210 and 227 total cells, respectively) revealed that patient cells had 2.0 times as many foci, with a false discovery rate of less than 5% (Figure 3c).
evidence: Quantified using BG4 Count program on immunofluorescence images (Figure 3).

claim: C9ALS patient fibroblasts contain on average 2.8 times as much BG4-stained area per cell than control fibroblasts.
source: Comparison of the average stained areas across the sets of cells through an unpaired t-test revealed that patient fibroblasts contained on average 2.8 times as much stained area per cell than did control fibroblasts, with a false discovery rate of less than 0.1%, while patient astrocytes had 2.3 times as much area, with a false discovery rate of less than 1.0% (Figure 3d).
evidence: Quantified using BG4 Count program on immunofluorescence images (Figure 3).

claim: C9ALS patient astrocytes have 2.3 times as much BG4-stained area as control astrocytes.
source: Comparison of the average stained areas across the sets of cells through an unpaired t-test revealed that patient fibroblasts contained on average 2.8 times as much stained area per cell than did control fibroblasts, with a false discovery rate of less than 0.1%, while patient astrocytes had 2.3 times as much area, with a false discovery rate of less than 1.0% (Figure 3d).
evidence: Quantified using BG4 Count program on immunofluorescence images (Figure 3).

claim: RNAse A treatment reduces the number of BG4 foci per cell by 27% in control patient astrocytes.
source: Treatment of astrocytes with RNAse A prior to BG4 antibody incubation in fact reduced the number of BG4 foci per cell, by 27% in the control patient cells and by a striking 76% in the C9ALS cells (relative to untreated control and C9 cells, respectively; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: RNAse A treatment reduces the number of BG4 foci per cell by 76% in C9ALS astrocytes.
source: Treatment of astrocytes with RNAse A prior to BG4 antibody incubation in fact reduced the number of BG4 foci per cell, by 27% in the control patient cells and by a striking 76% in the C9ALS cells (relative to untreated control and C9 cells, respectively; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The excess of BG4 foci observed in C9ALS patients is attributable to RNA G-Qs.
source: Given that the untreated C9ALS astrocytes in this experiment had 2.7 times as many foci per cell as untreated control cells, RNAse A treatment thus reduced both patient and control to nearly equivalent numbers of foci per cell (112 and 125 foci per cell, respectively), indicating that the excess of BG4 foci observed in the patients is in fact attributable to RNA G-Qs.
evidence: Inferred from RNAse A treatment results (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: The approximate incidence of nuclear colocalizing hnRNP H/BG4 foci in C9ALS astrocytes is 6.2%.
source: The approximate incidence of nuclear and cytoplasmic colocalizing foci detected in C9ALS astrocytes was 6.2 and 8.1%, respectively, and 0.4 and 2.6% in the control cells (Figure 4e).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: The approximate incidence of cytoplasmic colocalizing hnRNP H/BG4 foci in C9ALS astrocytes is 8.1%.
source: The approximate incidence of nuclear and cytoplasmic colocalizing foci detected in C9ALS astrocytes was 6.2 and 8.1%, respectively, and 0.4 and 2.6% in the control cells (Figure 4e).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: The approximate incidence of nuclear colocalizing hnRNP H/BG4 foci in control astrocytes is 0.4%.
source: The approximate incidence of nuclear and cytoplasmic colocalizing foci detected in C9ALS astrocytes was 6.2 and 8.1%, respectively, and 0.4 and 2.6% in the control cells (Figure 4e).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: The approximate incidence of cytoplasmic colocalizing hnRNP H/BG4 foci in control astrocytes is 2.6%.
source: The approximate incidence of nuclear and cytoplasmic colocalizing foci detected in C9ALS astrocytes was 6.2 and 8.1%, respectively, and 0.4 and 2.6% in the control cells (Figure 4e).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: Nuclear hnRNP H/BG4 colocalization was observed in 0.9% of C9ALS fibroblasts.
source: In fibroblasts, we counted 17 instances of high colocalization in the nuclei of C9ALS fibroblasts (Figure 4g), and 24 in the cytoplasm (Figure 4h), or 0.9% and 1.3%, respectively, for the ~1860 cells we counted.
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: Cytoplasmic hnRNP H/BG4 colocalization was observed in 1.3% of C9ALS fibroblasts.
source: In fibroblasts, we counted 17 instances of high colocalization in the nuclei of C9ALS fibroblasts (Figure 4g), and 24 in the cytoplasm (Figure 4h), or 0.9% and 1.3%, respectively, for the ~1860 cells we counted.
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: No nuclear hnRNP H/BG4 colocalization events were observed in control fibroblasts.
source: No nuclear colocalization events were observed in any of the ~1350 control fibroblasts, while cytoplasmic colocalization was observed in ~0.2% of cells (Figure 4i).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: Cytoplasmic hnRNP H/BG4 colocalization was observed in ~0.2% of control fibroblasts.
source: No nuclear colocalization events were observed in any of the ~1350 control fibroblasts, while cytoplasmic colocalization was observed in ~0.2% of cells (Figure 4i).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: RNAse A treatment increases nuclear hnRNP H/BG4 colocalization events in C9ALS astrocytes from 6.2% to 20%.
source: In support of this, when we counted colocalization events after RNAse A treatment in 44 patient astrocytes we found roughly the same rate of cytoplasmic colocalization events (9% after treatment as compared to 8.1% before), but more than three times as many nuclear colocalization events (20% after treatment compared to 6.2% before) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: C9ALS astrocytes have nonoverlapping hnRNP H foci in 18% of cells.
source: Specifically, C9ALS astrocytes had nonoverlapping hnRNP H foci in 18% of cells and control astrocytes had foci in 10% of cells (Figure 4e), while C9ALS fibroblasts had hnRNP H foci in 2.5% of cells and 1.1% of control fibroblasts had foci (Figure 4i).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: Control astrocytes have nonoverlapping hnRNP H foci in 10% of cells.
source: Specifically, C9ALS astrocytes had nonoverlapping hnRNP H foci in 18% of cells and control astrocytes had foci in 10% of cells (Figure 4e), while C9ALS fibroblasts had hnRNP H foci in 2.5% of cells and 1.1% of control fibroblasts had foci (Figure 4i).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: C9ALS fibroblasts have nonoverlapping hnRNP H foci in 2.5% of cells.
source: Specifically, C9ALS astrocytes had nonoverlapping hnRNP H foci in 18% of cells and control astrocytes had foci in 10% of cells (Figure 4e), while C9ALS fibroblasts had hnRNP H foci in 2.5% of cells and 1.1% of control fibroblasts had foci (Figure 4i).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: Control fibroblasts have nonoverlapping hnRNP H foci in 1.1% of cells.
source: Specifically, C9ALS astrocytes had nonoverlapping hnRNP H foci in 18% of cells and control astrocytes had foci in 10% of cells (Figure 4e), while C9ALS fibroblasts had hnRNP H foci in 2.5% of cells and 1.1% of control fibroblasts had foci (Figure 4i).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence images (Figure 4).

claim: In 36 C9ALS motor neurons, a total of 46 large hnRNP H foci were detected.
source: In the 36 C9ALS MNs we detected, we counted a total of 46 large hnRNP H foci, representing possible C9 RNA/hnRNP aggregates (see below).
evidence: Quantified from spinal cord immunohistochemistry (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: In 19 nonALS motor neurons, only three large hnRNP H foci were detected.
source: In contrast, in 19 nonALS MNs, we detected only three large hnRNP H foci.
evidence: Quantified from spinal cord immunohistochemistry (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: hnRNP H distribution is significantly altered in disease-relevant motor neuron populations in C9ALS patients.
source: We conclude that hnRNP H distribution is significantly altered in disease-relevant MN populations in C9ALS patients.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in hnRNP H foci between C9ALS and nonALS motor neurons.

claim: 12 out of 15 hnRNP H target exons showed decreased inclusion upon hnRNP H knockdown in U87 cells.
source: We found decreased exon inclusion following KD for 12/15 hnRNP H target transcripts (Figure 5d–l; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b–d), while three were unchanged (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a,e and f).
evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis (Figure 5).

claim: The skipped exon in WDR45 showed increased inclusion upon hnRNP H knockdown.
source: Unexpectedly, two of the three SRSF2 target exons, in WDR45 (Figure 5c) and PFKM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f), showed increased inclusion upon hnRNP H KD.
evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis (Figure 5c).

claim: The exon in PFKM showed increased inclusion upon hnRNP H knockdown.
source: Unexpectedly, two of the three SRSF2 target exons, in WDR45 (Figure 5c) and PFKM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f), showed increased inclusion upon hnRNP H KD.
evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1f).

claim: 11 of the 12 hnRNP H targets that changed following knockdown in U87 cells displayed similar changes in C9ALS samples compared to controls.
source: Strikingly, 11 of the 12 hnRNP H targets and one of the two SRSF2 targets that changed following KD in U87 cells displayed similar changes in the C9ALS samples compared to controls (Figure 5c–l, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c; note that for two exons, in ARRB2 and KIAA1542, p values were 0.065 and 0.081, respectively).
evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis of patient brain samples (Figure 5).

claim: CLIP tags were found within 200 bps of 17 out of 18 exons that differed between nonALS and C9ALS.
source: Indeed, we found CLIP tags within 200 bps of 17 out of 18 exons that differed between nonALS and C9ALS, with the only exception being the exon in ATXN2, for which CLIP tags were present within 500 bp.
evidence: Analyzed from published hnRNP H CLIP-seq data (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).

claim: Only one hnRNP A1 target exon, in ZCCHC17, differed significantly between C9ALS and nonALS brains.
source: Only one exon, in ZCCHC17, differed significantly, and it was more excluded in C9ALS patients relative to nonALS, opposite the outcome that would be predicted if hnRNP A1 levels were reduced.
evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: Shorter disease duration correlated with greater changes in exon inclusion.
source: Interestingly, this trend also reflected disease duration, i.e., time from onset of symptoms until death, for each patient, a rough indicator of disease severity (Supplementary file 1). Shorter disease duration correlated with greater changes in exon inclusion, suggesting that hnRNP H splicing dysregulation is a marker of clinical progression.
evidence: Inferred from linear regression analysis (Figure 5m) and patient clinical data.

claim: hnRNP H splicing dysregulation is a marker of clinical progression.
source: Shorter disease duration correlated with greater changes in exon inclusion, suggesting that hnRNP H splicing dysregulation is a marker of clinical progression.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between disease duration and splicing changes.

claim: The average percentage of insoluble hnRNP H is 30.0% in nonALS motor cortex.
source: The average percentage of insoluble hnRNP H was 30.0% in nonALS and 56.1% in C9ALS (p=0.013).
evidence: Determined by biochemical fractionation and western blotting (Figure 6a, b).

claim: The average percentage of insoluble hnRNP H is 56.1% in C9ALS motor cortex.
source: The average percentage of insoluble hnRNP H was 30.0% in nonALS and 56.1% in C9ALS (p=0.013).
evidence: Determined by biochemical fractionation and western blotting (Figure 6a, b).

claim: There is 1.9 times as much insoluble hnRNP H in the motor cortex of C9ALS patients as compared to control.
source: We conclude that there is 1.9 times as much insoluble hnRNP H in the motor cortex of C9ALS patients as compared to control, providing evidence that hnRNP H sequestration by C9 repeats occurs in the brains of ALS patients to a biochemically significant level.
evidence: Calculated from biochemical fractionation data (Figure 6b).

claim: On average, 2.7 times as much hnRNP H co-immunoprecipitated with BG4 from C9ALS samples as from nonALS controls.
source: We found, on average, 2.7 times as much hnRNP H co-IPed from the C9ALS samples as from the nonALS controls (Figure 6d) (p=0.0007).
evidence: Determined by BG4 co-IP from insoluble fractions (Figure 6c, d).

claim: No SR proteins were detected in BG4 co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Using an antibody that recognizes a common phospho-epitope on all SR proteins, we did not detect co-IP of any SR proteins (Figure 6c).
evidence: Shown by western blotting of BG4 IP samples (Figure 6c).

claim: hnRNP H forms aggregates with G-Qs in the brains of C9ALS patients.
source: We conclude that hnRNP H forms aggregates with G-Qs in the brains of C9ALS patients, providing additional evidence that hnRNP H is indeed sequestered by C9 G-Q RNA, and to an extent sufficient to bring about the observed splicing dysregulation.
evidence: Inferred from BG4 co-IP results showing hnRNP H association with G-Q structures in insoluble fractions.

claim: A number of proteins have been suggested to bind the C9 transcribed repeats.
source: However, while a number of proteins have been suggested to bind the transcribed repeats (Haeusler et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Cooper-Knock et al., 2014), the functional significance of such binding is not well established.
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Haeusler et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Cooper-Knock et al., 2014).

claim: The list of possible C9 repeat binding proteins includes hnRNP A3, SRSF1, Pur alpha, ADARB2, SRSF2, hnRNP H, hnRNP A1, ALYREF, nucleolin and RanGAP.
source: The list of possible C9 repeat binding proteins currently includes hnRNP A3 (Mori et al., 2013a), SRSF1 (Lee et al., 2013; Reddy et al., 2013; Zamiri et al., 2014), Pur alpha (Rossi et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2013), ADARB2 (Donnelly et al., 2013), SRSF2 (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013), hnRNP H (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013), hnRNP A1 (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Zamiri et al., 2014), ALYREF (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014), nucleolin (Haeusler et al., 2014) and RanGAP (Zhang et al., 2015b).
evidence: Compiled from multiple cited studies.

claim: Only SRSF1, hnRNP H and nucleolin have been suggested to bind RNA G-Qs among the proposed C9 binding proteins.
source: Of these proteins, only SRSF1, hnRNP H and nucleolin have been suggested to bind RNA G-Qs (von Hacht et al., 2014); however, the known binding specificities of SRSF1 and nucleolin appear inconsistent with high affinity binding to GGGGCC repeats (Tacke and Manley, 1995; Ghisolfi-Nieto et al., 1996), and our results did not provide evidence for SR proteins binding C9 RNA.
evidence: Based on cited literature (von Hacht et al., 2014; Tacke and Manley, 1995; Ghisolfi-Nieto et al., 1996) and experimental results.

claim: A meta-analysis of independent RNA pulldown studies identified hnRNP H1 or hnRNP H3 as the proteins most consistently found associated with C9 RNA.
source: Moreover, a meta-analysis of independent RNA pulldown studies identified hnRNP H1 or the highly related hnRNP H3 as the proteins most consistently found associated with C9 RNA (Haeusler et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous work (Haeusler et al., 2016).

claim: Exons that respond to hnRNP H knockdown with significantly lowered inclusion show enrichment of G-runs within 70 bases downstream of their 5' splice site.
source: KD of hnRNP H followed by RNA-seq revealed that exons that respond with significantly lowered inclusion show enrichment of G-runs within 70 bases downstream of their 5' splices site (Xiao et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from previous work (Xiao et al., 2009).

claim: A positive correlation exists between the extent of change in exon inclusion and the number of G's in G-runs downstream of the 5' splice site.
source: Moreover, a positive correlation between the extent of the change in inclusion and the number of G's in these G-runs was observed, and larger changes in splicing following KD were detected for exons with relatively weak 5' splice sites.
evidence: Cited from previous work (Xiao et al., 2009).

claim: Sequencing of RNA from C9ALS patient brains revealed global changes in alternative splicing, particularly skipping of exons enriched for putative hnRNP H binding motifs.
source: Indeed, sequencing of RNA from C9ALS patient brains revealed global changes in alternative splicing, particularly skipping of exons that are proximally enriched for putative hnRNP H binding motifs (Prudencio et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous work (Prudencio et al., 2015).

claim: ATXN2 encodes a polyglutamine protein associated with spinocerebellar ataxia 2.
source: For example, ATXN2 encodes a polyglutamine protein associated with spinocerebellar ataxia 2 (Imbert et al., 1996) and contains an expansion that also confers increased susceptibility to ALS in sporadic (Elden et al., 2010), and possibly C9 (van Blitterswijk et al., 2014), cases.
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Imbert et al., 1996; Elden et al., 2010; van Blitterswijk et al., 2014).

claim: ATXN2 contains an expansion that confers increased susceptibility to ALS in sporadic cases.
source: For example, ATXN2 encodes a polyglutamine protein associated with spinocerebellar ataxia 2 (Imbert et al., 1996) and contains an expansion that also confers increased susceptibility to ALS in sporadic (Elden et al., 2010), and possibly C9 (van Blitterswijk et al., 2014), cases.
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Elden et al., 2010; van Blitterswijk et al., 2014).

claim: GABBR1 encodes one of the subunits of the heterodimeric GABA receptor B.
source: Additionally, GABBR1 encodes one of the subunits of the heterodimeric GABA receptor B (GABABR).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GABBR1.

claim: When exon 19 of GABBR1 is skipped, a frameshift occurs, likely reducing levels of GABBR1 protein.
source: When exon 19 is skipped, as we observed in patient brains, a frameshift occurs, likely reducing levels of GABBR1 protein.
evidence: Inferred from the observed exon skipping and knowledge of frameshift consequences.

claim: GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian CNS.
source: GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian CNS (Gassmann and Bettler, 2012) and reduced GABA-mediated inhibition may contribute to excitotoxic cell death in ALS (Brockington et al., 2013), which may provide a molecular basis for the potentially pathogenic finding of cortical hyperexcitability in C9ALS patients (Geevasinga et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Gassmann and Bettler, 2012; Brockington et al., 2013; Geevasinga et al., 2015).

claim: Reduced GABA-mediated inhibition may contribute to excitotoxic cell death in ALS.
source: GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian CNS (Gassmann and Bettler, 2012) and reduced GABA-mediated inhibition may contribute to excitotoxic cell death in ALS (Brockington et al., 2013), which may provide a molecular basis for the potentially pathogenic finding of cortical hyperexcitability in C9ALS patients (Geevasinga et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous work (Brockington et al., 2013).

claim: The extent of splicing dysregulation is inversely correlated with disease duration.
source: While there is no conclusive data establishing causality for any of the multiple mechanisms proposed to explain the toxicity of the C9 repeats, our data and that of others (Cooper-Knock et al., 2015) suggest that the extent of splicing dysregulation, in our case specifically of hnRNP H targets, is inversely correlated with disease duration, or directly correlated with disease severity.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation analysis (Figure 5m) and cited work (Cooper-Knock et al., 2015).

claim: Over time, RNA transcribed from the C9 repeats accumulates to levels sufficient to titrate cellular supplies of hnRNP H, leading to splicing defects.
source: We propose that over time, RNA transcribed from the C9 repeats eventually accumulates to levels sufficient to titrate cellular supplies of hnRNP H, thus leading to splicing defects of target transcripts.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Longer-lived, postmitotic neurons would not have the advantage of clearing RNA-protein aggregates.
source: While deleterious consequences arising from missplicing might be tolerated or avoided in dividing cells that can regenerate before hnRNP H levels become sufficiently low, longer-lived, postmitotic neurons would not have the advantage of clearing RNA-protein aggregates, which may themselves have toxic consequences for the cell.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the age-dependent nature of the disease.

claim: In neurons, sequestration of hnRNP H becomes more severe with time and continuing C9 transcription.
source: We predict that in neurons, sequestration of hnRNP H becomes more severe with time and continuing C9 transcription, until functional levels become low enough to deregulate splicing, providing an explanation for the age dependence of ALS/FTD.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claim: The most prevalent aggregations in ALS are ubiquitinated, cytoplasmic inclusions containing TDP-43.
source: The most prevalent aggregations in ALS are ubiquitinated, cytoplasmic inclusions containing TDP-43, which occur in the brain and spinal cord of virtually all ALS patients, with the exception of SOD1 and FUS ALS cases.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the ALS field.

claim: The only aggregates unique to C9 are p62/ubiquitin-positive, TDP-43-negative cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions containing DPRs.
source: Thus far, the only aggregates unique to C9 are p62/ubiquitin-positive, TDP-43-negative cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions containing DPRs derived from non-ATG translation of expanded C9 transcripts (Blokhuis et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous work (Blokhuis et al., 2013).

claim: DPRs can display neurotoxic properties.
source: Such DPRs can display neurotoxic properties (Mizielinska et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2014), consistent with a role in MN death in ALS.
evidence: Cited from previous studies (Mizielinska et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2014).

claim: DPRs are enriched in non-vulnerable brain regions and largely absent from the spinal cord of C9ALS patients.
source: However, it has been reported that they are enriched in non-vulnerable brain regions and largely absent from the spinal cord of C9ALS patients, raising questions regarding their exact role in motor neuron degeneration (Davidson et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous work (Davidson et al., 2015).

claim: This study provides the first evidence that G-Q expansions bound to hnRNP H form insoluble aggregates in disease-relevant regions of the brain.
source: Our experiments thus provide the first evidence that G-Q expansions bound to hnRNP H indeed form insoluble aggregates, and are present in disease-relevant regions of the brain.
evidence: Based on the biochemical fractionation and co-IP experiments (Figure 6).
